title: Ch. 3 — Speaking with Names
paragraphs: The epigraph is Barrie Greenbie: what each of us actually experiences of the landscape is selected, shaped and coloured by what we know. Basso opens by describing the condition of the newcomer, for whom an unfamiliar landscape and an unfamiliar language arrive together — emphatically there, sensory and inescapable, yet lacking any accustomed order, and so keenly disconcerting. The ethnographer's task is first to learn to listen, and then to see freshly.

He then reproduces a conversation he could not understand at the time. In Lola Machuse's kitchen, a guest called Louise describes her younger brother's illness: months earlier, working a cattle roundup at Trail Extends Into A Grove Of Sticklike Trees, he stepped on a snakeskin wedged between rocks. A crewman warned him that contact with snakes is always dangerous and urged him to see a snake medicine person at once. He smiled and said no harm would come to him. Louise is plainly worried, and has to pause to regain her composure.

What follows is almost entirely place-names. Lola says: it happened at Line Of White Rocks Extends Up And Out, at this very place. A silence of thirty to forty-five seconds. Emily answers: yes, it happened at Whiteness Spreads Out Descending To Water, at this very place. Another silence. Lola again: truly, it happened at Trail Extends Across A Red Ridge With Alder Trees, at this very place. Louise laughs softly. Robert Machuse says gozh doleeł — pleasantness and goodness will be forthcoming — and Lola repeats it. Louise then remarks that her younger brother is foolish, addressing the observation to the dog. The talk stops, and everyone retreats into their own thoughts.

Each name carries a tale, and each tale pictures a carelessness. The first is about a girl living with her maternal grandmother who was told always to avoid the rocky canyon where snakes lived; hot and thirsty and unwilling to carry heavy firewood the long way, she went down through the canyon anyway, slipped, and scattered her load. Nobody in the kitchen mentions the brother, and nobody draws the parallel. Lola's own explanation is the clearest statement of the practice in the book: that woman was too sad and worried too much about her younger brother, so we tried to make her feel better and think good thoughts. He acted stupidly and failed to show respect — but we said nothing critical about him to her. We talked around it. Those place-names are strong.

Behind the practice is a theory of mind cast in visual terms. Speaking gives evidence of thinking, thinking happens in the form of pictures, and speaking is the work of depicting those pictures so that hearers, on hearing and holding the words, can view them in their own minds. Discourse is therefore a reciprocal exchange of depicted pictures — and the depictions are treated as projects to complete. This is why economy is a virtue and volubility an offence. A person who describes too busily, supplies too many details, repeats and qualifies too often, smothers the audience: the arrogant message is that you must see everything exactly as I do. Such a speaker insults the imagination of others and holds down their minds. An effective narrator opens up thinking, so that listeners can travel.

So Lola's summary of what they achieved is exact: we gave that woman pictures to work on in her mind, we did not speak too much, we did not hold her down — that way she could travel in her mind and add on to them easily. Her mind went to those places and stood in front of them as the ancestors did long ago. Basso's more general point is that landscapes are available to their inhabitants in symbolic as well as material terms, and can therefore be detached from their spatial moorings and put to interactional work: statements about the land conveying tacit messages about the relationships of the people talking. The ethnographic challenge is to fathom what a landscape can be called upon to say — and what, through the saying, it can be called upon to do.
